drivingQuestion: What does 'noladim' mean in a vow, and how is R' Meir's view to be read?
outcomeNote: Resolved: the word is ambiguous and vows follow common speech.

segments.he: גְּמָ׳ לְרַבִּי מֵאִיר וְלָא מִיבַּעְיָא נוֹלָדִים. אֶלָּא מִמַּאן אָסוּר?
segments.en: «GEMARA:» The Gemara comments: «According to Rabbi Meir,» in the case of one who takes a vow that deriving benefit from those who will be born is forbidden to him, the halakha is that he is permitted to derive benefit even from those who are already born at the time of the vow. «And» the mishna’s use of the term: Even, indicates that «it is not necessary» to say that those who «will be born» are permitted to him. The Gemara asks: «However,» if that is the case, «from whom is he prohibited» to derive benefit? The vow appears to have no effect.

segments.he: חַסּוֹרֵי מִיחַסְּרָא וְהָכִי קָתָנֵי: הַנּוֹדֵר מִן הַיְּלוּדִים — מוּתָּר בַּנּוֹלָדִים, מִן הַנּוֹלָדִים — אָסוּר בַּיְּלוּדִים, רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: אַף הַנּוֹדֵר מִן הַנּוֹלָדִים מוּתָּר בַּיְּלוּדִים, כִּי הֵיכִי דְּנוֹדֵר מִן הַיְּלוּדִים מוּתָּר בַּנּוֹלָדִים.
segments.en: The Gemara answers: The mishna «is incomplete and is teaching like this: One who takes a vow» not to derive benefit «from those that are born» is «permitted» to derive benefit from «those who will be born» after the time of the vow. But if one takes a vow not to derive benefit «from those who will be born,» he is also «prohibited» from deriving benefit «from those that are» already «born» at the time of the vow. «Rabbi Meir says: Even one who takes a vow» not to derive benefit «from those who will be born» is «permitted» to derive benefit «from those who are» already «born, just as one who takes a vow» not to derive benefit «from those who are born» is «permitted» to derive benefit «from those who will be born,» because Rabbi Meir claims that the one taking the vow was precise in his words.

segments.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב פָּפָּא לְאַבָּיֵי: לְמֵימְרָא דְּ״נוֹלָדִים״ דְּמִתְיַילְּדָן מַשְׁמַע? אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה ״שְׁנֵי בָנֶיךָ הַנּוֹלָדִים לְךָ בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם״, הָכִי נָמֵי דְאִיתְיַילְדָן הוּא?
segments.en: With regard to the distinction between the terms in the mishna, «Rav Pappa said to Abaye: Is this to say that» the word «noladim means those who will be born» in the future? «But if that is so,» it says in the verse: «“Your two sons who were born [noladim] to you in the land of Egypt”» (Genesis 48:5), «does it also» mean «those who will be born?» The verse is referring to Manasseh and Ephraim, who were already alive.

segments.he: וְאֶלָּא מַאי דִּיילִידוּ מַשְׁמַע, אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה דִּכְתִיב ״הִנֵּה בֵן נוֹלָד לְבֵית דָּוִד יֹאשִׁיָּהוּ שְׁמוֹ״, הָכִי נָמֵי דַּהֲוָה? וְהָא עֲדַיִין מְנַשֶּׁה לֹא בָּא? אֶלָּא מַשְׁמַע הָכִי וּמַשְׁמַע הָכִי, וּבִנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם.
segments.en: The Gemara responds: «But rather, what» should one say; «that» the expression «means those already born? However, if that is so,» that «which is written: “Behold, a son shall be born [nolad] to the house of David, Josiah by name”» (I Kings 13:2), is the meaning «also that he is already» born? «But Manasseh had not yet come» into this world, and certainly not his grandson Josiah. «Rather,» sometimes the word «means this,» those already born, «and» sometimes «means that,» those who are not yet born, «and with regard to vows, follow the colloquial language,» in which the word noladim is used to mean those who are not yet born, so the vow is interpreted in this manner.
